question: The unacceptable decision of ‘Hellenic Train’ to summon an employee, unionist Nikos Tsaklidis, on the outrageous accusation that he ‘caused a service anomaly’, was taken on the grounds of his refusal to perform the coupling-uncoupling of carriages and engines, which requires the participation of two employees, alone.
The EU and Greek governments’ policy of ‘liberalisation’ and privatisation of rail transport has resulted in the intensification of work and the exposure of employees and passengers to risks.

Can the Commission say: What is its position on the fact that, more than two and a half years after the Tempi disaster/crime, the railway network continues to face a lack of safety measures and staff as a result of the EU’s strategy – implemented by the Greek governments – for the liberalisation and privatisation of rail transport (Directive 2012/34 and Directive 2016/798), based on ‘costbenefit’ criteria, competitiveness and the profitability of groups?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) With regard to the effect of liberalisation on rail safety, the Commission notes that the available data does not confirm a negative impact on safety of the opening of the railway market to competition.

A stable positive trend of improvement of safety levels can be observed in the Single European Railway Area since 2010 – as evidenced by data on safety performance collected by the European Union Agency for Railways (ERA).

According to this data, the number of significant accidents has dropped from 2230 in 2010 to 1565 in 2023, a similar downward trend can be observed for the number of victims of these accidents (fatalities and seriously injured). Most of the reported accidents refer to accidents caused by third parties: level crossings users and unauthorised persons crossing the railway tracks.

These two categories of accidents account also for 97,4% of all fatalities1. With regard to the rail safety in Greece, the Commission deplores the tragic accident in Tempi. Shortly after the accident, the Commission requested ERA to prepare a report on the state of implementation of the rail safety legislation in Greece.

On that basis, the Commission opened an infringement case INFR(2023)20362 against Greece which addresses several longstanding shortcomings in the functioning of the Greek rail system. To address them, the Greek authorities have developed an Action Plan, which contains measures strengthening the capacity of the infrastructure manager to adequately carry out its responsibilities.
The Commission, together with ERA, are in a continuous dialogue with the Greek authorities on the implementation of the Action Plan while the actions envisaged there are closely monitored.
